description: CEO/Board strategic document format vault. Written documents only — no slides, no presentations. Each format has structure, rules, and when to use it.

amazon_6pager_crisis.name: Amazon 6-Pager (Crisis Variant)
amazon_6pager_crisis.origin: Amazon. Jeff Bezos banned PowerPoint in 2004. All meetings start with 20 minutes of silent reading.
amazon_6pager_crisis.when: Strategic decision under time pressure. The reader needs to understand the full situation AND make a decision in one sitting.
amazon_6pager_crisis.why_it_works: Forces the writer to think in complete sentences. No hiding behind bullet points. The narrative structure means the reader builds understanding progressively — they can't skip to the recommendation without understanding why.
amazon_6pager_crisis.page_count: 3-5 pages (original Amazon is 6, but crisis briefs are tighter)
amazon_6pager_crisis.font: 11pt body, 14pt section headers. One font throughout (Inter or similar sans-serif). No bold except section headers and the recommendation line.

structure.purpose: What happened and why the reader is holding this document
structure.constraints: 3-5 sentences. No jargon. A reader who missed the last month of news should understand. End with: why this matters to the reader's organization specifically.
structure.example_opener: On February 28, Iran mined the Strait of Hormuz in response to US-Israeli strikes...

structure.purpose: The specific question this document answers
structure.constraints: One paragraph. Must be a QUESTION, not a statement. Name the decision-maker, the domain, the timeframe, and the constraint. Include the decision sensitivity — the number at which the recommendation reverses.
structure.example: Within the next 7 days, what should IOCL and HMEL decide regarding crude procurement and fiscal backstop — given that the current $156/bbl crude price generates $100M/day in losses against frozen retail prices, and this recommendation reverses if crude drops below $124/bbl?

structure.purpose: The 4-6 core assertions that answer the problem statement
structure.constraints: Each hypothesis is one paragraph. State the claim, the evidence, the break point, and the confidence level. Mark each as CONFIRMED, UNCERTAIN, or KILLED. Include 1-2 killed hypotheses to show rigor. Reference appendix slides inline where a chart proves the claim.
structure.format_per_hypothesis: Claim in bold first sentence. Evidence in 2-3 sentences. Break point: 'This reverses if [specific condition].' Confidence: HIGH/MEDIUM/LOW with one-line basis.

structure.purpose: The specific actions required, in sequence
structure.constraints: Numbered list. Each decision is ONE action, ONE owner, ONE deadline. Start with a verb: Approve, Authorize, Direct, Confirm. Under 30 words each. State dependencies: 'Requires Decision 1 to be completed first.' No compound decisions.

structure.purpose: Explicit list of data needed before the recommendation is actionable
structure.constraints: Numbered list. Each gap names: what is needed, who provides it, by when, and which decision it blocks. This section is not optional — every strategic document has unknowns. Hiding them destroys credibility.
structure.why_important: The CEO needs to know what can go wrong. Omitting data gaps signals either ignorance or dishonesty.

formatting_rules: Single-spaced body text, double-space between sections
Section headers left-aligned, bold, 14pt
Body text 11pt, regular weight
No bullet points in Context or Hypotheses — full prose paragraphs
Decisions and Data Gaps use numbered lists
No colors anywhere except: RED for killed hypothesis status, GREEN for confirmed
No charts, no tables, no boxes, no cards — those go in the appendix
Inline appendix references in parentheses: (see Appendix 2)
Page numbers bottom-right
Footer: 'Developed by [name]' centered, grey, small

mckinsey_memo.name: McKinsey Strategic Memo
mckinsey_memo.origin: McKinsey & Company. Minto Pyramid Principle. Conclusion-first, then evidence.
mckinsey_memo.when: Strategic recommendation where the reader is a senior executive who wants the answer first, then the reasoning.
mckinsey_memo.why_it_works: Pyramid structure means the reader can stop at any point and have a complete (if less detailed) understanding. The first sentence answers the question. Everything after defends it.

structure.purpose: First paragraph IS the answer. No preamble.
structure.constraints: 2-3 sentences. State what to do, why, and the key number. Example: 'IOCL should draw emergency credit lines today and secure the UAE cargo by April 4. Without these two actions, a $26B debt default becomes structurally probable by April 13.'
structure.rule: If you cover the rest of the memo, the reader should still know what to do from this paragraph alone.

structure.purpose: Establish stakes in 2-3 sentences
structure.constraints: One anchor number. What happens if nothing is done. No history lesson — only what the reader needs to understand the recommendation.

structure.purpose: 3-5 findings that prove the recommendation. These ARE the hypotheses.
structure.constraints: Each finding is one paragraph. Bold first sentence is the finding. Remaining sentences are evidence. Each ends with 'so what' — the implication for the decision.
structure.rule: Reading just the bold first sentences of all findings should tell the complete story.

structure.purpose: What could go wrong and what to do about it
structure.constraints: 2-3 risks. Each names the trigger, the impact, and the contingency action. Include the hypothesis graveyard (what was tested and killed).

structure.purpose: Specific actions with owners and deadlines
structure.constraints: Numbered. Atomic. Verb-first. Sequenced.

formatting_rules: No section header for the opening recommendation — it just starts
Remaining section headers: bold, left-aligned, no numbering
Body: 11pt, single-spaced
Bold first sentence of each finding paragraph
No colors, no boxes, no design elements
Appendix references inline

military_sitrep.name: Military SITREP / BLUF
military_sitrep.origin: US Military. Bottom Line Up Front. Used in intelligence briefings, situation reports, and commander's updates.
military_sitrep.when: Situation update where the reader needs to know the current state and what changed since last update. Not primarily a decision document.
military_sitrep.why_it_works: BLUF means the most important information comes first. The reader can stop after the first paragraph and take action. Details follow for those who need them.

structure.purpose: The single most important thing the reader needs to know
structure.constraints: 2-3 sentences maximum. State: what happened, what it means, what action is needed. No background — jump straight to the point.

structure.purpose: Minimum context needed to understand the BLUF
structure.constraints: One paragraph. Only include what changed since the reader last looked at this topic.

structure.purpose: The data that supports the BLUF
structure.constraints: Numbered list. Each fact is one sentence. Source in parentheses. Confidence flagged if uncertain.

structure.purpose: What the facts mean — analyst judgment
structure.constraints: 1-2 paragraphs. Distinguish between 'we know' and 'we assess' (opinion). State assumptions explicitly.

structure.purpose: What to do
structure.constraints: Numbered actions. Direct language: 'Approve X' not 'It is recommended that X be considered.'

formatting_rules: BLUF label in bold caps at top
Monospace font acceptable for classification markings
No design elements — pure text document
Can be transmitted via email or printed on paper with identical readability

board_paper.name: Corporate Board Paper
board_paper.origin: Standard corporate governance. UK Corporate Governance Code, ASX guidelines, Indian Companies Act board practices.
board_paper.when: Formal board approval is required. Legal/regulatory document that becomes part of board minutes.
board_paper.why_it_works: Structured for governance: the board needs to know what they're approving, why, what the risks are, and what authority they're delegating. Legal teams review these.

structure.purpose: One sentence: what the board is being asked to approve
structure.constraints: Example: 'To approve emergency procurement authority of up to $1.8B per contract for crude oil purchases.'

structure.purpose: Context the board needs
structure.constraints: 1-2 paragraphs. Factual. No advocacy — save that for Recommendation.

structure.purpose: What alternatives were evaluated
structure.constraints: 2-3 options. Each with pros, cons, and financial impact. The recommended option should be obvious from the analysis, not stated until the next section.

structure.purpose: What management recommends and why
structure.constraints: Clearly state the recommended option and the key reasons. Reference the options analysis.

structure.purpose: Quantified P&L, cash flow, and balance sheet impact
structure.constraints: Table format. Show impact under base case and stress case.

structure.purpose: Key risks and mitigants
structure.constraints: Table: Risk, Likelihood, Impact, Mitigant. 3-5 risks maximum.

structure.purpose: The exact wording the board is asked to approve
structure.constraints: Legal language. 'RESOLVED THAT the Board hereby approves...' This goes into board minutes.

formatting_rules: Formal tone throughout
Section numbers: 1., 2., 3., etc.
Tables for financial impact and risk assessment
No informal language, no contractions
Annexures for supporting detail (these are the appendix slides)
Classification marking on every page

note: The pipeline should ask the user which format to use, or auto-select based on brief_type (crisis -> amazon_6pager_crisis, strategic -> mckinsey_memo, update -> military_sitrep, board_approval -> board_paper)
